Also note that as voltage increases, current decreases. This action produces what is called negative resistance in the area between points B and C.
Biasing a tunnel diode between points B and C allows a small change in bias voltage, input, to produce a large change in current flow, output.
It is the area between points B and C, which is non-linear, that gives the tunnel diode amplification properties.
After the barrier potential voltage is reached, the tunnel diode operates as a conventional diode with a linear change in current flow.
From points B to C, the tunneling decreases causing current to decrease.
From points A to B, the tunneling increases causing current to increase.
The flow is due to the thin PN junction. Electrons "tunnel" through the junction barrier causing current.
Tunnel diodes have a sharp increase in current flow followed by a non-linear decrease in current flow before the barrier potential voltage is reached.
Recall that a conventional diode, when forward biased, produces a linear raise in current flow after the barrier potential voltage has been exceeded.
The high concentration of impurities produces a thin PN junction barrier that causes tunnel diodes to operate differently than conventional diodes.
Tunnel diodes are PN junction devices with a very high concentration of impurities in both the P and N regions.
The tunnel diode is a diode that operates as an amplifier or oscillator at microwave frequencies.
The next special microwave semiconductor device is the tunnel diode.
